title: Neurologic Imaging in a Patient with Cirrhosis and Altered Mental Status: To CT or Not to CT
case_prompt:
A 61-year-old woman with cirrhosis secondary to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis presented with a one-month history of increased intermittent confusion and emotional lability. Three months earlier, she had been started on lactulose 30 mL three times daily for presumed hepatic encephalopathy, yet she continued to have episodes of confusion, anxiety, and emotional instability. She also reported occasional shakiness and episodes in which she did not recognize her husband or children. 

On examination, she was awake, alert, and oriented to person, place, and date but was confused about why she was in the hospital and exhibited a tangential thought process. A full neurologic examination showed no cranial nerve deficits, no focal motor or sensory deficits, normal deep tendon reflexes, and no asterixis. 

Laboratory studies revealed an ammonia level of 98 µmol/L and a MELD-Na score of 14. She was continued on lactulose, and rifaximin was added.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Hepatic encephalopathy was considered given her cirrhosis and elevated ammonia, but her symptoms persisted despite lactulose therapy — “Despite adherence to lactulose, she continued to have episodes of confusion, anxiety and emotional lability.”  
2. Cerebrovascular accident was included in the differential for altered mental status in cirrhosis but was not supported by imaging findings — “the differential diagnosis includes etiologies such as cerebrovascular accident … which can present with similar symptoms to HE.”  
3. Intracerebral hemorrhage was considered due to coagulopathy risk in cirrhosis, but imaging did not demonstrate bleeding — “the differential diagnosis includes etiologies such as … intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) … all of which can present with similar symptoms to HE.”  
4. Structural brain lesion became the leading diagnosis when neuroimaging revealed an extra-axial mass consistent with a meningioma — “A head CT scan … showed a left frontal convexity extra-axial lesion … suspicious for a meningioma.”
